packet.current_instruction:
Let’s try that with the library returns note.

**With the volunteer line**
New volunteers, here’s how to sort returns.
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

**Without the volunteer line**
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

Scan each version once for a blue-dot return and once for an unmarked return. Which version helps you find both actions faster? Then write your own version and explain one edit that helps a new volunteer decide where a return goes.
earlier_instruction: “The side door” gives a first-time visitor a specific entrance to look for, and “by 6 p.m. Friday” tells them when to arrive. Your explanation shows why the edit matters: the visitor can act on the notice without knowing the café’s routine. For practice, rewrite the notice for a first-time volunteer using the same brief. Which detail would you change, and what would you need to ask before giving the volunteer an arrival time?

Your choice fits the spot you pictured. Beside the main door, the notice tells a first-time visitor with a lamp where to go next. If the notice were farther away and the visitor saw volunteers entering first, ‘Volunteers use the main entrance’ could help them understand why they should head to the side door. Try writing a version for that spot using only facts from the brief. I’ve noted ‘Writing clear directions for first-time readers’ as your revisit topic here.
packet.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer

learner_history.first_answer:
Bringing a lamp to the repair café? Please use the side door and arrive by 6 p.m. Friday.

I changed “the usual entrance” to “the side door” because a first-time visitor wouldn’t know which entrance we usually use.
learner_history.return_request: Can we try two versions of the lamp notice, one with the line about volunteers and one without? I want to see which is easier to scan.
learner_history.surprise: I almost added “Volunteers use the main entrance” because I pictured a visitor seeing people go in there and following them. I left it out because I pictured my notice taped beside the main door, where the lamp instruction would be the first thing they saw. Yes, please save writing clear directions for first-time readers as a topic.

packet.new_task: Write a short onboarding note for a new library volunteer shelving returns. Items with a blue dot stay on the cart for staff to check. Unmarked items go on the shelves. The draft says, 'Put the returns where they belong.' Revise it in your own voice and explain one edit that helps the new volunteer decide what to do.

response.response:
The version without the volunteer line felt a little faster for both. I could go straight to the marks.

Blue dot? Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
No mark? Put it on the shelf.

I put the mark first on each line so a new volunteer can match what they see on the return to where it goes.
